fact.instrument: Agreement of Dec. 28, 1886, ratified by Act of May 1, 1888, ch. 213, 25 Stat. 113
fact.note: The instrument reads: “the separate reservation for the Indians now attached to and receiving rations at the, Fort Peck Agency, Montana, shall be bounded as follows”. Agreement (Dec. 28, 1886) ratified by Congress; it carves the separate Fort Peck reservation out of the larger Gros Ventre, Piegan, Blood, Blackfeet and River Crow reservation created by Exec. Order of July 5, 1873 (1 Kappler 855-856), which does not name the Assiniboine or Sioux. The act names "Indians now attached to ... Fort Peck Agency," not the Assiniboine and Sioux Tribes by name.

fact.land_area: La Pointe band tract (Bad River), Wisconsin
fact.instrument: Treaty of La Pointe, Sept. 30, 1854, art. II, 10 Stat. 1109
fact.note: The instrument reads: “2d. For the La Pointe band, and such other Indians as may see fit to settle with them, a tract of land bounded as follows”. Tract runs from near the Montreal River to Chequamegon (Shag-waw-me-quon) Point; Bad River Reservation as identified by modern boundaries. Buffalo's subdivision (Red Cliff) is covered by clause 6.

The instrument reads: “be set apart as a reservation for the Gros Ventre, Piegan, Blood, Blackfeet, River Crow, and other Indians”. Substantially reduced by Exec. Order of Aug. 19, 1874 and the Act of Apr. 15, 1874 (18 Stat. 28), and later the Act of May 1, 1888 (cited in Kappler as 25 Stat. 129); the 1855 Treaty (11 Stat. 657) created a common hunting ground, not a reservation. Order text begins on p. 855 and ends on p. 856.

fact.instrument: Treaty with the Bois Forte Band, Apr. 7, 1866, art. III, 1st, 14 Stat. 765-766
fact.note: The instrument reads: “for the perpetual use and occupancy of said Bois Forte band of Chippewas, a tract of land of not less than one hundred thousand acres”. The treaty directed selection of a tract including Nett Lake; The treaty only authorized selection of the tract; the later instruments that fixed the Nett Lake and Deer Creek lands were not located here. Recorded as the first authorization.

fact.land_area: Cahuilla Reservation, San Diego County (now Riverside County), California
fact.note: The instrument reads: “Cahuila. — Township 7 south, range 2 east ... withdrawn from sale and set apart as reservations for the permanent use and occupancy of the Mission Indians in Lower California”. The order lists the tract as "Cahuila"; Kappler heading groups all 1875 tracts as Mission Indian reservations. Later orders (1877-1891) enlarged it.

fact.land_area: Capitan Grande Reservation, San Diego County, California
fact.note: The instrument reads: “Capitan Grande. — Township 14 south, range 2 east ... withdrawn from sale and set apart as reservations for the permanent use and occupancy of the Mission Indians in Lower California”. The Barona and Viejas groups derive from this reservation (separate roster entries not recorded here).

fact.land_area: Great Sioux Reservation (the land of the Cheyenne River Reservation lies within it)
fact.instrument: Treaty with the Sioux, Apr. 29, 1868, art. II, 15 Stat. 635, 636
fact.note: The instrument reads: “shall be, and the same is, set apart for the absolute and undisturbed use and occupation of the Indians herein named”. The treaty set apart the Great Sioux Reservation (the district between the east bank of the Missouri, the Nebraska line, the 104th meridian and the 46th parallel); the separate Cheyenne River Reservation was carved from it by the Act of Mar. 2, 1889. Treaty is the first instrument for this land.

The instrument reads: “is hereby set apart for a permanent reservation for the Indians receiving rations and annuities at the Cheyenne River Agency”. Separate reservation created from the Great Sioux Reservation.

fact.land_area: Rocky Boy's Reservation (about 56,035 acres of the former Fort Assinniboine Military Reservation), Montana
fact.note: The instrument reads: “apart as a reservation for Rocky Boy’s Band of Chippewas and such other homeless Indians in the State of Montana”. An earlier appropriation act authorized the Secretary to settle Rocky Boy's Band on public land or purchase land; it did not itself set land aside.

fact.land_area: Cocopah Reservation (west half of sec. 12 and related lands), Arizona
fact.note: The instrument reads: “withdrawn and set apart for the use and occupancy of the Cocopah Indians”. Earliest order located; heading "Cocopah" in Kappler vol. 4, Part III.

fact.land_area: Northern Idaho reservation for the Coeur d'Alenes and other tribes
fact.note: The instrument reads: “Let the lands be set apart as reservations for the Indians within named, as recommended by the Acting Secretary of the Interior.”. The accompanying recommendation sets apart a northern reservation (about 20 miles square) for "the Cœur d'Alenes and other tribes of northern Idaho" (1 Kappler 836); the reservation was not actually established on the ground until the Exec. Order of Nov. 8, 1873. Low confidence that the 1867 tract is the same land.

The instrument reads: “withdrawn from sale and set apart as a reservation for the Cœur d’Alene Indians, in said Territory”. First order naming a Coeur d'Alene reservation; enlarged by later orders and the act of Mar. 3, 1891 (26 Stat. 1027).

fact.land_area: Colorado River Reservation (Arizona), lands west of a line from Half-Way Bend to Corner Rock
fact.note: The instrument reads: “shall be set apart for an Indian reservation for the Indians of said river and its tributaries”. Kappler: Colorado River Reserve "established by act of March 3, 1865 (13 Stat., 559), and following Executive orders" (1 Kappler 803). Enlarged by Exec. Orders of Nov. 22, 1873, Nov. 16, 1874 and May 15, 1876.

fact.instrument: Treaty of Hell Gate, July 16, 1855, art. II, 12 Stat. 975
fact.note: The instrument reads: “There is, however, reserved from the lands above ceded, ... for the use and occupation of the said confederated tribes, and as a general Indian reservation”. Kappler lists the Jocko Reserve (Flathead Agency) as "established by treaty July 16, 1855" (1 Kappler 859).

fact.instrument: Treaty with the Yakama, June 9, 1855, art. II, 12 Stat. 951, 952
fact.note: The instrument reads: “There is, however, reserved, from the lands above ceded ... for the use and occupation of the aforesaid confederated tribes and bands of Indians, the tract of land included within the following boundaries”. Ratified Mar. 8, 1859; proclaimed Apr. 18, 1859. Kappler also lists the Yakima reserve as established by this treaty and by later orders.

The instrument reads: “The reservation of the land within denoted by blue-shaded lines is hereby made”. Kappler gives the order under "Siletz (originally known as Coast) Reserve." Conditional reservation for the Coast tribes; curtailed by Exec. Order of Dec. 1866 and Act of Mar. 3, 1875 (18 Stat. 446). The Siletz Reservation was terminated in 1956 and restored in 1977; the current Census area is trust land.

fact.land_area: Chehalis Reserve (selection at the mouth of the Black River), Washington Territory
fact.instrument: Order of the Sec'y of the Interior, July 8, 1864, 1 Kappler 903
fact.note: The instrument reads: “I approve the suggestion made in relation to the subject, and you are hereby authorized and instructed to purchase the improvements of D. Mounts”. Approval of the superintendent's selection of a reservation of about six sections; not an executive order. Exec. Order of Oct. 1, 1886 (1 Kappler 903) refers to the tract "reserved for the use and occupation of the Chehalis Indians, by order of the Secretary of the Interior, dated July 8, 1864" and restored part of it to the public domain.

The instrument reads: “named in communication of the Commissioner of Indian Affairs dated the 8th instant, and for such other Indians as the Department of the Interior may see fit to locate thereon”. Printed under the heading "Colville Reserve." The Commissioner's letter (1 Kappler 915) names the Methow, Okanagan, San Poel, Lake, Colville, Calispel, Spokane and Coeur d'Alene bands, "not parties to any treaty." This tract (Columbia River to the Pend d'Oreille/Clark River) was replaced three months later by the July 2, 1872 order.

fact.land_area: Colville Reserve (as it stands, bounded by the Columbia and Okanogan Rivers), Washington Territory
fact.note: The instrument reads: “be, and the same is hereby, set apart as a reservation for said Indians, and for such other Indians as the Department of the Interior may see fit to locate thereon”. The order restores the Apr. 9 tract to the public domain and, "in lieu thereof," sets apart the country bounded east and south by the Columbia River, west by the Okanogan River and north by the British possessions. Reduced later (Moses/Columbia Reserve, Act of July 1, 1892, 27 Stat. 62).

The instrument reads: “set aside for the use and benefit of the Goshute and other Indians on the public domain in the State of Utah”. First order naming the Goshute located and read in Kappler; it follows a small agency tract set aside by Exec. Order No. 1539 (May 29, 1912, T. 11 S., R. 19 W.) that does not name the Goshute and whose Kappler page was not found. The Nevada portion of the Goshute Reservation is not covered by this order.

fact.instrument: Executive indorsement of President Buchanan, June 30, 1857, 1 Kappler 886
fact.note: The instrument reads: “withdrawn from sale and entry and set apart as a reservation for Indian purposes till otherwise ordered”. The 1904 print's OCR gives the year as 1867; the earlier print and the signer (James Buchanan) show 1857. The order does not itself name Grande Ronde; Kappler's heading "Grande Ronde Reserve" and the Secretary's letter ("Willamette tribes, parties to treaty of January, 1855") identify it. Grand Ronde descends from the Treaties of Jan. 22, 1855 (Molala etc.) and Dec. 21, 1855.

fact.instrument: Treaty with the Walla-Wallas, Cayuses, and Umatilla, June 9, 1855, art. I, 12 Stat. 945, 946
fact.note: The instrument reads: “shall be set apart as a residence for said Indians”. Article I cedes the country and sets apart the described tract "shall be held and regarded as an Indian reservation" beginning on the Umatilla River.

fact.land_area: Warm Springs Reservation (tract beginning at the De Chutes River), Oregon
fact.instrument: Treaty with the Tribes of Middle Oregon, June 25, 1855, art. I, 12 Stat. 963, 964
fact.note: The instrument reads: “shall, until otherwise directed by the President of the United States, be set apart as a residence for said Indians”. Boundaries described beginning "in the middle of the channel of the De Chutes River opposite the eastern termination of a range of high lands usually known as the Mutton Mountains."

The instrument reads: “is hereby set apart for a permanent reservation for the Indians receiving rations and annuities at the Crow Creek Agency”. The act treats the Crow Creek tract as part of the Great Sioux Reservation, but the Crow Creek Reserve had earlier existed on the east bank of the Missouri (Kappler Part III, not read for this land); original instrument therefore unconfirmed (original=false).

fact.land_area: Crow Reservation, Montana Territory (107th meridian to the Yellowstone)
fact.instrument: Treaty with the Crows, May 7, 1868, art. II, 15 Stat. 649, 650
fact.note: The instrument reads: “shall be, and the same is, set apart for the absolute and undisturbed use and occupation of the Indians herein named”. Later changed by Exec. Orders of Oct. 20, 1875 and Mar. 8, 1876, the Act of Apr. 11, 1882 and the agreement of 1891/1892 (Kappler 1 Kappler 857-859).

fact.instrument: Treaty of Fort Bridger, July 3, 1868, art. II, 15 Stat. 673, 674
fact.note: The instrument reads: “shall be and the same is set apart for the absolute and undisturbed use and occupation of the Shoshonee Indians herein named”. Boundaries run from the mouth of Owl Creek along the Wind River Mountains. The Northern Arapaho are not party to this treaty (see doubtful list).

fact.instrument: Treaty of La Pointe, Sept. 30, 1854, art. II, 10 Stat. 1110
fact.note: The instrument reads: “For the Fond Du Lac bands, a tract of land bounded as follows”. Kappler: Fond du Lac Reservation "established by treaty September 30, 1854" (1 Kappler 850).

fact.instrument: Agreement of Jan. 21, 1887, ratified by Act of May 1, 1888, ch. 213, 25 Stat. 113
fact.note: The instrument reads: “the separate reservation for the Indians now attached to and receiving rations at the Fort Belknap Agency shall be bounded as follows”. Carved out of the reservation of Exec. Order of July 5, 1873 (1 Kappler 855-856). The act names "Indians now attached to ... Fort Belknap Agency," not the Gros Ventre and Assiniboine by name.
The instrument reads: “reserved for the Camp or Fort Independence Indians entitled to allotments thereon”. 320.40 acres.

fact.land_area: Gila River (Pima and Maricopa) Reservation, Arizona
fact.note: The instrument reads: “authorized and required to set apart the tract ... or tracts of land aforesaid as a reservation for the confederated bands of ... Pimas and Maricopas”. Congress directed the President to set apart the surveyed Gila River tracts as a reservation (not exceeding 100 square miles); Kappler lists the Gila River Reserve as "established by act of February 28, 1859 (11 Stat., 401), and Executive orders" (1 Kappler 804, 805). The act is a mandate to the President; I have not found a separate order recording the original set-aside, so the act is treated as the original instrument. Enlarged by EOs beginning Aug. 31, 1876.

fact.instrument: Treaty of La Pointe, Sept. 30, 1854, art. II, 10 Stat. 1110
fact.note: The instrument reads: “For the Grand Portage band, a tract of land bounded as follows”. Kappler: Grand Portage Reserve "established by treaty September 30, 1854" (1 Kappler 850).

The instrument reads: “withdrawn from sale and settlement, and set apart for the use and occupancy of said Suppai Indians”. Replaced by the order of Nov. 23, 1880 (same page), which redefined the boundaries; Suppai = Havasupai (Kappler heading "Suppai (Havasupai) Reserve").
The instrument reads: “withdrawn from sale and settlement and set apart as a reservation for the Hoh Indians not now residing upon any Indian reservation”.

fact.instrument: Proclamation of Austin Wiley, Superintendent of Indian Affairs for California, Aug. 21, 1864 (under Act of Apr. 8, 1864, 13 Stat. 39), 1 Kappler 815
fact.note: The instrument reads: “I have this day located an Indian reservation ... Settlers in Hoopa Valley are hereby notified”. Located by the California Superintendent under the Act of Apr. 8, 1864, 13 Stat. 39 (which authorized up to four reservations), "subject to the approval of the President." The day is legible in the earlier Kappler print (Fort Gaston, Aug. 21, 1864); the 1904 print's OCR gives "August 1861" (the year is 1864). Boundaries were fixed by Exec. Order of June 23, 1876. Page 815 per the running page number.

fact.land_area: Hoopa Valley Indian Reservation, California (89,572.43 acres)
fact.note: The instrument reads: “declared to be the exterior boundaries of Hoopa Valley Indian Reservation”. Confirms the Hoopa Valley Reservation as one of the reservations authorized by the Act of Apr. 8, 1864 (13 Stat. 39) and fixes its boundaries. Extended along the Klamath River by Exec. Order of Oct. 16, 1891.

The instrument reads: “withdrawn from settlement and sale, and set apart for the use and occupancy of the Moqui and such other Indians as the Secretary of the Interior may see fit to settle thereon”. Moqui = Hopi (Kappler heading "Moqui (Hopi) Reserve").
The instrument reads: “set aside and reserved for the use and occupancy of the Hualpai Indians”. Date of the order is Jan. 4, 1883 per OSU record; the Kappler OCR prints "January 1883".

fact.land_area: Inaja and Cosmit Reservation, San Diego County, California
fact.note: The instrument reads: “Inaja. — Township 13 south, range 3 east ... withdrawn from sale and set apart as reservations for the permanent use and occupancy of the Mission Indians in Lower California”. The order also lists "Cosmit" (OCR reads "Gosmit") as a separate tract; the roster nation holds the combined Inaja and Cosmit Reservation.

fact.land_area: Jicarilla Apache Reserve (Colorado line to the Navajo reservation), New Mexico
fact.note: The instrument reads: “set apart as a reservation for the Jicarilla Apache Indians by the first article of an agreement concluded with the said Indians December 10, 1873, subject to the action of Congress”. Revoked July 18, 1876; the reservation was re-established by Exec. Orders of Sept. 21, 1880 (revoked May 15, 1884) and Feb. 11, 1887 (1 Kappler 875), the order of Feb. 11, 1887 being the one that created the present core of the reservation.

The instrument reads: “set aside for use of the Kaibab and other Indians now residing thereon”. An earlier order, Exec. Order No. 1786 (a temporary withdrawal of Arizona lands), was not read in full; this is the earliest order located that names the Kaibab.
The instrument reads: “set aside as a reservation for the Kalispel Indians in that State”. The order itself sets the land aside for the Kalispel Indians.

fact.land_area: L'Anse and Vieux Desert tracts, Michigan
fact.instrument: Treaty of La Pointe, Sept. 30, 1854, art. II, 10 Stat. 1109
fact.note: The instrument reads: “1st. For the L’Anse and Vieux De Sert bands, all the unsold lands in the following townships in the State of Michigan”. Art. II: "The United States agree to set apart and withhold from sale, for the use of the Chippewas of Lake Superior, the following described tracts of land." Kappler lists L'Anse Reserve as established by this treaty (1 Kappler 847).

fact.land_area: Lac du Flambeau and Lac Court Oreilles tracts, Wisconsin
fact.instrument: Treaty of La Pointe, Sept. 30, 1854, art. II, 10 Stat. 1110
fact.note: The instrument reads: “a tract of land lying about Lac De Flambeau, and another tract on Lac Court Orielles, each equal in extent to three townships”. Boundaries to be fixed later under the President's direction.

fact.land_area: Lac du Flambeau and Lac Court Oreilles tracts, Wisconsin
fact.instrument: Treaty of La Pointe, Sept. 30, 1854, art. II, 10 Stat. 1110

The instrument reads: “is hereby set apart for a permanent reservation for the Indians receiving rations and annuities at the Lower Brule Agency”. Separate reservation created from the Great Sioux Reservation.

fact.instrument: Treaty of Point Elliott, Jan. 22, 1855, art. II, 12 Stat. 927, 928
fact.note: The instrument reads: “the island called Chah-choo-sen, situated in the Lummi River”. Lummi Reservation enlarged by Exec. Order of Nov. 22, 1873.

fact.instrument: Treaty with the Makah, Jan. 31, 1855, art. II, 12 Stat. 939
fact.note: The instrument reads: “the following tract of land, viz.: Commencing on ... the beach at the mouth of a small brook running into Neah Bay”. Enlarged by Exec. Orders of Oct. 26, 1872 (replaced Jan. 2, 1873) and Oct. 21, 1873.

fact.land_area: Fort Stanton Indian Reserve (Mescalero Apache), New Mexico
fact.note: The instrument reads: “be set apart as a reservation for the Mescalero Apache Indians, as recommended by the Secretary of the Interior and Commissioner of Indian Affairs”. Cancelled and replaced by the Exec. Order of Feb. 2, 1874 (same page range), which set apart different lands "for the use of said Mescalero Apaches and such other Indians as the Department may see fit to locate thereon."

The instrument reads: “the following-described lands in the southeastern part of Nevada are hereby set apart for the use of the Indians in that locality”. Cancelled and replaced by the Exec. Order of Feb. 12, 1874 (1 Kappler 867); Kappler also cites act of Mar. 13, 1875 (18 Stat. 445).

The instrument reads: “withdrawn from sale or other disposition, and set apart as the Muckleshoot Indian Reservation, for the exclusive use of the Indians in that locality”. The order says it is "supplemental to the action of the Department approved by the President January 20, 1857" (Medicine Creek treaty lands); that 1857 action was not located, so it is possible the 1857 action was the true first set-aside.

fact.instrument: Treaty with the Navajo, June 1, 1868, art. II, 15 Stat. 667, 668
fact.note: The instrument reads: “shall be, and the same is hereby, set apart for the use and occupation of the Navajo tribe of Indians”. Kappler lists the Navajo Reserve as established by treaty and later Executive orders (1 Kappler 805, 875); Utah and later additions by Exec. Orders.

fact.instrument: Treaty with the Nez Perces, June 11, 1855, art. II, 12 Stat. 957
fact.note: The instrument reads: “There is, however, reserved from the lands above ceded ... for the use and occupation of the said tribe, and as a general reservation”. Reduced by the treaty of June 9, 1863, 14 Stat. 647 (the 1863 article again sets apart a reservation in the Clearwater country) and later acts.

fact.land_area: Nisqually tract near the mouth of She-nah-nam Creek, Washington
fact.instrument: Treaty of Medicine Creek, Dec. 26, 1854, art. II, 10 Stat. 1132
fact.note: The instrument reads: “a square tract containing two sections, or twelve hundred and eighty acres, on Puget’s Sound, near the mouth of the She-nah-nam Creek”. Treaty tract identified with the Nisqually reservation by location (She-nah-nam = Sequalitchew/Nisqually); the later Exec. Order of Jan. 20, 1857 enlarged it (not read).

The instrument reads: “set apart as a reservation for the use and occupation of the Northern Cheyenne Indians”. Kappler: "established by Executive orders only." Enlarged and redefined by Exec. Order of Mar. 19, 1900 (1 Kappler 860-861) and later orders.

fact.land_area: San Juan Pueblo (Ohkay Owingeh) land grant, New Mexico
fact.note: The instrument reads: “the Pueblo land claims in the Territory of New Mexico designated in the corrected lists as ... C, Pueblo of San Juan in the county of Rio Ariba ... be, and they are hereby, confirmed”. Congress confirmed the Pueblo's land claim (Spanish-era grant) as reported by the New Mexico surveyor general and directed the Commissioner of the General Land Office to survey and issue a patent. The act confirms an existing Spanish/Mexican grant rather than setting land aside de novo; the underlying Spanish grant dates are not given in the act. Later patents (1864 onward) and additions by executive order/statute are not covered here.

fact.note: The instrument reads: “which is reserved by the ... for their future home”. Reserve described as the country "north of said due west line".

fact.land_area: Pala Reservation, San Diego County, California

fact.land_area: Puyallup tract on the south side of Commencement Bay, Washington
fact.instrument: Treaty of Medicine Creek, Dec. 26, 1854, art. II, 10 Stat. 1132
fact.note: The instrument reads: “a square tract containing two sections, or twelve hundred and eighty acres, lying on the south side of Commencement Bay”. Puyallup Reservation enlarged by Exec. Orders including Sept. 6, 1873 (1 Kappler 923).

fact.instrument: Letter of Comm'r of Indian Affairs, Nov. 29, 1859, 1 Kappler 868
fact.note: The instrument reads: “reserving from sale and settlement, for Indian use, a tract of land in the northern portion of the valley of the Truckee River, including Pyramid Lake”. Administrative reservation requested of the General Land Office ("to respect said reservations upon the plats of survey"); not an executive order, but Kappler prints it as the first act in the reserve's history, and the Exec. Order of Mar. 23, 1874 later confirmed the surveyed reservation. It is recorded as the original set-aside, though its legal form is a Commissioner's reservation.

The instrument reads: “the tract of country known and occupied as the Pyramid Lake Indian Reservation in Nevada, as surveyed by Eugene Monroe, in January, 1865”. Confirms and sets apart by order the surveyed reservation (withdrawn from sale and set apart for the Pah-Ute and other Indians residing thereon).

fact.land_area: Yuma Reserve (Arizona side of the Colorado River opposite the Gila mouth)
fact.note: The instrument reads: “withdrawn from settlement and sale and set apart as a reservation for the Yuma and such other Indians as the Secretary of the Interior may see fit to settle thereon”. This Arizona tract was cancelled and replaced by the Exec. Order of Jan. 9, 1884 (1 Kappler 832) setting apart lands in California; the Fort Yuma Reservation as it exists is the Jan. 9, 1884 tract. Kappler also notes the act of Aug. 15, 1894 (28 Stat. 332).

The instrument reads: “In lieu of an Executive order dated July 6, 1883, setting apart certain lands in the Territory of Arizona as a reservation for the Yuma Indians, which order is hereby cancelled”. Replacement order; tract in California except the Fort Yuma military reservation.

The instrument reads: “withdrawn from sale and settlement and set apart for the permanent use and occupation of the Quillehute Indians”. Quillehute = Quileute. The 1873 Quinaielt order also named the Quillehute among the tribes for whom that reserve was set apart, but the Quileute Reservation proper at La Push dates from this order.

The instrument reads: “be withdrawn from sale and set apart for the use of the Quinaielt, Quillehute, Hoh, Quit, and other tribes of fish-eating Indians on the Pacific coast”. Issued under the Treaty of Olympia (July 1, 1855 and Jan. 25, 1856, 12 Stat. 971), which provided for a reservation to be selected by the President but did not itself describe the tract.

fact.instrument: Treaty of La Pointe, Sept. 30, 1854, art. II, cl. 6, 10 Stat. 1109, 1110
fact.note: The instrument reads: “The Ontonagon band and that subdivision of the La Pointe band of which Buffalo is chief, may each select on or near the lake shore, four sections of land”. Red Cliff is the reservation of Buffalo's band; actual lands were selected and set aside after the treaty (survey/Exec. action not read).

fact.land_area: Potrero tract including Rincon, San Diego County, California
fact.note: The instrument reads: “Portrero. — Including Rincon ... withdrawn from sale and set apart as reservations for the permanent use and occupancy of the Mission Indians in Lower California”. The tract is headed "Portrero" (Potrero) and "Including Rincon, Gapich, and La Joya"; Rincon is named. "La Joya" is not matched here to La Jolla (see doubtful).

fact.land_area: Great Sioux Reservation (the land of the Rosebud Reservation lies within it)
fact.instrument: Treaty with the Sioux, Apr. 29, 1868, art. II, 15 Stat. 635, 636
fact.note: The instrument reads: “shall be, and the same is, set apart for the absolute and undisturbed use and occupation of the Indians herein named”. The treaty set apart the Great Sioux Reservation (the district between the east bank of the Missouri, the Nebraska line, the 104th meridian and the 46th parallel); the separate Rosebud Reservation was carved from it by the Act of Mar. 2, 1889. Treaty is the first instrument for this land.

The instrument reads: “is hereby set apart for a permanent reservation for the Indians receiving rations and annuities at the Rosebud Agency”. Separate reservation created from the Great Sioux Reservation.

fact.instrument: Order of the Secretary of the Interior (Nov. 18, 1858), as recited in Commissioner's letter of Jan. 6, 1860, 1 Kappler 824-825
fact.note: The instrument reads: “the entire valley of Nome Cult, designated by you as the Round Valley, was set apart and reserved for Indian purposes”. The Nov. 18, 1858 Commissioner's letter to Superintendent Henley (1 Kappler 824-825) conveys the Secretary's direction that "the entire Nome Cult Valley shall be retained as a reservation." The 1860 letter cited is the source read for the quotation. Later made one of the Act of Apr. 8, 1864 (13 Stat. 39) reservations; boundaries fixed by Exec. Orders (1870 onward). Not an executive order or statute in the first instance; confidence low.

fact.land_area: Salt River lands (Pima and Maricopa Reserve), Arizona
fact.note: The instrument reads: “it is hereby ordered that there be withdrawn from sale and settlement and set apart for the use of said Pima and Maricopa Indians, as an addition to the reservation set apart for said Indians by act of Congress”. Kappler cross-references the Salt River Reserve to this order ("See Pima and Maricopa or Gila River Res., Ex. order June 14 1879", 1 Kappler 808). The order is framed as an addition to the Gila River reservation and replaced an order of Jan. 10, 1879; the tract lies north of the Gila around the Salt River.

fact.land_area: San Carlos division of the White Mountain Indian Reservation, Arizona
fact.note: The instrument reads: “withheld from sale and added to the White Mountain Indian Reservation in said Territory, which addition shall hereafter be known as the “San Carlos division of the”. Original instrument for the San Carlos land; it added the San Carlos division to the White Mountain Reservation (later separately administered as San Carlos). Later orders (1873-77) restored parts to the public domain.

fact.land_area: Pueblo of Santo Domingo (Kewa) land grant, New Mexico
fact.note: The instrument reads: “the Pueblo land claims in the Territory of New Mexico designated in the corrected lists as ... H, Pueblo of Santo Domingo in the county of Santa Ana ... be, and they are hereby, confirmed”. Congress confirmed the Pueblo's land claim (Spanish-era grant) as reported by the New Mexico surveyor general and directed the Commissioner of the General Land Office to survey and issue a patent. The act confirms an existing Spanish/Mexican grant rather than setting land aside de novo; the underlying Spanish grant dates are not given in the act. Later patents (1864 onward) and additions by executive order/statute are not covered here.

The instrument reads: “reserved from sale and set apart for Indian purposes”. Order does not itself name the Shoalwater; Kappler's heading "Shoalwater Reserve" (and OSU) identify it, and Kappler records it as occupied by Shoalwater and Chehalis. Date Sept. 22, 1866 per OSU; Kappler prints "September 1866".

fact.land_area: Fort Hall Reserve (southern Idaho reservation for the Boise and Bruneau Shoshones and Bannocks)
fact.note: The instrument reads: “Let the lands be set apart as reservations for the Indians within named, as recommended by the Acting Secretary of the Interior.”. The recommendation printed with the order describes the southern reservation as "The Boise and Bruneau bands of Shoshones and Bannock Reservation ... comprehending Fort Hall" (1 Kappler 836). The July 30, 1869 order (1 Kappler 839) designated this tract as the Bannock reservation under the Treaty of July 3, 1868; Kappler: "This reservation is included in the executive order of June 14, 1867" (1 Kappler 838). Fort Hall boundaries later changed by treaty and acts.

fact.land_area: Duck Valley Reserve, Idaho and Nevada
fact.note: The instrument reads: “And the above-named tract of land is hereby set apart as a reservation for the Western Shoshone Indians”. Order is printed under the Nevada heading "Duck Valley Reserve"; enlarged by Exec. Order of May 4, 1886 (adding lands for the Paddy Cap band of Pi-Utes).

fact.instrument: Treaty with the Sisseton and Wahpeton, Feb. 19, 1867, art. III, 15 Stat. 505, 506
fact.note: The instrument reads: “shall be set apart for the members of said bands who have heretofore surrendered to the authorities of the government ... the following described lands as a perma nent reservation”. Art. IV set apart a separate reservation (Devils Lake, now Spirit Lake) for other members and the Cuthead Yanktonai; that is not the roster nation here.

fact.land_area: Reservation of six sections at the head of Hood's Canal, Washington
fact.instrument: Treaty of Point No Point, Jan. 26, 1855, art. II, 12 Stat. 934 (art. II begins at 933)
fact.note: The instrument reads: “amount of six sections, or three thousand eight hundred and forty acres, situated at the head of Hood’s Canal, to be hereafter set apart”. The preamble names the S'Klallam villages and the Sko-ko-mish, Too-an-hooch and Chem-a-kum tribes. The tract was 'to be hereafter set apart' and was fixed later by Exec. Order of Feb. 25, 1874.

The instrument reads: “withdrawn from sale or other disposition and set apart for the use of the S’Klallam Indians the following tract of country on Hood’s Canal”. Describes the tract beginning at the mouth of the Skokomish River, inclusive of the six treaty sections.
The instrument reads: “set aside for the use of certain Skull Valley Indians now residing thereon”. About 17,920 acres.

fact.land_area: Ute Reservation, Colorado Territory (west of the 107th meridian)
fact.instrument: Treaty with the Ute, Mar. 2, 1868, art. II, 15 Stat. 619
fact.note: The instrument reads: “shall be, and the same is hereby, set apart for the absolute and undisturbed use and occupation of the Indians herein named”. The present Southern Ute and Ute Mountain Ute reservations were carved from this reservation under the Act of June 15, 1880 (21 Stat. 199) (not read here); the treaty is the first instrument for the land base.

The instrument reads: “set aside and reserved for the use and occupancy of the Spokane Indians”. The tract lies between Chamokane Creek, the Spokane River and the Columbia River. Exec. Order of Apr. 9, 1872 (Colville) had earlier listed the Spokane among beneficiaries of a different tract.

fact.instrument: Treaty of Medicine Creek, Dec. 26, 1854, art. II, 10 Stat. 1132
fact.note: The instrument reads: “The small island called Klah-che-min, situated opposite the mouths of Hammersley’s and Totten’s inlets”. Art. II: "There is, however, reserved for the present use and occupation of the said tribes and bands, the following tracts of land."

fact.land_area: Great Sioux Reservation (the land of the Standing Rock Reservation lies within it)
fact.instrument: Treaty with the Sioux, Apr. 29, 1868, art. II, 15 Stat. 635, 636
fact.note: The instrument reads: “shall be, and the same is, set apart for the absolute and undisturbed use and occupation of the Indians herein named”. The treaty set apart the Great Sioux Reservation (the district between the east bank of the Missouri, the Nebraska line, the 104th meridian and the 46th parallel); the separate Standing Rock Reservation was carved from it by the Act of Mar. 2, 1889. Treaty is the first instrument for this land.

The instrument reads: “is hereby set apart for a permanent reservation for the Indians receiving rations and annuities at the Standing Rock Agency”. Separate Standing Rock Reservation created from the Great Sioux Reservation; Exec. Orders of Mar. 16, 1876 and Mar. 20, 1884 (1 Kappler 884) had earlier added/restored east-of-Missouri lands for the Standing Rock Agency.

fact.instrument: Treaty of Point Elliott, Jan. 22, 1855, art. II, 12 Stat. 927, 928
fact.note: The instrument reads: “surrounding the small bight at the head of Port Madison, called by the Indians Noo-sohk-um”. Art. II reserves tracts "for the present use and occupation of the said tribes and bands"; Port Madison tract is "the amount of two sections ... surrounding the small bight at the head of Port Madison."

fact.instrument: Treaty of Point Elliott, Jan. 22, 1855, art. II, 12 Stat. 927, 928
fact.note: The instrument reads: “the peninsula at the southeastern end of Perry’s Island called Shais-quihl”. Exec. Order of Sept. 9, 1873 (1 Kappler 925) fixed the northern boundary of the "Swinomish Reservation."

fact.land_area: Sycuan Reservation, San Diego County, California
fact.note: The instrument reads: “Sycuan. — Township 16 south, range 1 east ... withdrawn from sale and set apart as reservations for the permanent use and occupancy of the Mission Indians in Lower California”. Section 13 only.

The instrument reads: “set aside for the use of two certain bands of homeless Shoshone Indians now residing near the towns of Winnemucca and Battle Mountain”. Battle Mountain Band tract (NW 1/4 and NW 1/4 NE 1/4 sec. 18, T. 32 N., R. 45 E., and further lands in T. 32 N., R. 44 E.).
The instrument reads: “set aside for the use of certain Shoshone and Paiute Indians now residing near the town of Elko, Nevada”. Order does not name the Te-Moak Tribe; 160 acres near Elko.

fact.land_area: Fort Berthold Reserve (Arickaree, Gros Ventre and Mandan Reservation), Dakota Territory
fact.note: The instrument reads: “Let the lands indicated in the accompanying diagram be set apart as a reservation for the Arickaree, Gros Ventre, and Mandan Indians”. Kappler's 1880 order (1 Kappler 883) calls it "the Arickaree, Gros Ventre, and Mandan Reservations set aside by Executive order dated April 12, 1870, and known as the Fort Berthold Reservation." The order is undated in Kappler's OCR ("April 1870") but refers to the Interior letter of the 12th. The Fort Laramie treaty of Sept. 17, 1851 had described a larger territory for these tribes but Kappler lists it as unratified/amended.

fact.land_area: Papago Indian Reserve (San Xavier del Bac), Arizona
fact.note: The instrument reads: “to be known as the Papago Indian Reserve.”. First reservation set apart for the Papago (Tohono O'odham); the same order says "set apart for the use of the Papago and such other Indians as it may be desirable to place thereon, the following tract of country around San Xavier del Bac" (1 Kappler 805). The much larger main Tohono O'odham reservation was set aside later (see separate entry).

fact.land_area: Gila Bend Reserve (T. 5 S., R. 5 W., Gila and Salt River meridian), Arizona
fact.note: The instrument reads: “withdrawn from sale and settlement and set apart for the use and occupancy of the Papago and other Indians now settled there”. Second Papago tract; separate land base (now the Gila Bend reservation of the Tohono O'odham Nation); original=false because the San Xavier order (1874) came first.

fact.land_area: Tulalip (Snohomish) tract on Port Gardner/Tulalip Bay, Washington
fact.instrument: Treaty of Point Elliott, Jan. 22, 1855, art. II, 12 Stat. 927, 928
fact.note: The instrument reads: “on the north side Hwhomish Bay and the creek emptying into the same called Kwilt-seh-da”. The Dec. 23, 1873 Exec. Order (1 Kappler 925) refers to "the Snohomish or Tulalip Indian Reservation ... provided for in the third article of the treaty ... Point Elliott" [sic]. Place-name identification (Kwilt-seh-da = Tulalip Bay) is from the treaty text as reproduced; confidence medium.

The instrument reads: “Let the lands described in the within letter be set apart as a reservation for the bands of Indians in California therein named”. Canceled and replaced "in lieu" by the Exec. Order of Oct. 3, 1873 for the same bands.

The instrument reads: “set apart as a reservation for the Tule River, King’s River, Owen’s River, Manche Cajon, and other scattered bands of Indians in the State of California”. Replaces the Jan. 9, 1873 tract; later enlarged by Exec. Orders (1878, 1886).

The instrument reads: “withdrawn from sale and settlement and set apart for the use and occupancy of the Turtle Mountain band of Chippewas”. Restored in large part to the public domain by the Exec. Order of Mar. 29, 1884 (townships 162-163 N. excepted), and amended June 3, 1884 (1 Kappler 885); the later treaty/agreement of 1892 and acts affect the reservation.

The instrument reads: “that the Uintah Valley, in the Territory of Utah, be set apart and reserved for the use and occupancy of Indian tribes”. President Lincoln's order reads "Let the reservation be established, as recommended by the Secretary of the Interior." Kappler cites the Acts of May 5, 1864 (13 Stat. 63) and May 24, 1888 (25 Stat. 157). The Uncompahgre Reserve (Exec. Order of Jan. 5, 1882) was added for the Uncompahgre Utes.

fact.land_area: Ute Reservation, Colorado Territory (west of the 107th meridian)
fact.instrument: Treaty with the Ute, Mar. 2, 1868, art. II, 15 Stat. 619
fact.note: The instrument reads: “shall be, and the same is hereby, set apart for the absolute and undisturbed use and occupation of the Indians herein named”. The present Southern Ute and Ute Mountain Ute reservations were carved from this reservation under the Act of June 15, 1880 (21 Stat. 199) (not read here); the treaty is the first instrument for the land base.

fact.instrument: Letter of Comm'r of Indian Affairs, Nov. 29, 1859, 1 Kappler 868
fact.note: The instrument reads: “a tract in the northeastern part of the valley of W alker’s River, including Walker’s Lake”. Same 1859 letter reserves a tract including Walker's Lake; the surveyed Walker River reservation was set apart by Exec. Order of Mar. 19, 1874. Quote OCR spacing ("W alker") is preserved from the scan.

The instrument reads: “the reservation situated on Walker River, Nevada, as surveyed by Eugene Monroe, December, 1864”. Withdrawn from public sale and set apart for the Pah-Ute Indians residing thereon; first order directly establishing the surveyed reservation.

fact.instrument: Treaty with the Chippewa of the Mississippi, Mar. 19, 1867, art. II, 16 Stat. 719, 720
fact.note: The instrument reads: “there is hereby set apart for their use a tract of land, to be located in a square form as nearly as possible ... which reservation shall include White Earth Lake and Rice Lake, and contain thirty-six townships of land”. Treaty also reserves a tract for the Mississippi bands (Gull Lake / Mille Lacs, Leech Lake) in art. I.

The instrument reads: “that the President issue an order authorizing said tracts of country described in Mr. Colyer’s letter to be regarded as reservations”. Kappler prints the Nov. 7, 1871 Interior Secretary recommendation (p. 811, naming the Camp Apache tract in the White Mountains selected for the Coyotero and Chilicco Apaches) with the President's Nov. 9 referral directing the Secretary of War to carry out the recommendations (p. 812). Kappler's heading is "White Mountain or San Carlos Reserve"; the Camp Apache tract had earlier been set apart administratively by the War Department (the Sept. 5, 1871 letter on p. 810 says the White Mountain region "has been set apart by the War Department"). No separate order text names the reservation until Dec. 14, 1872.

The instrument reads: “Respectfully referred to the Secretary of War, who will take such action as may be necessary to carry out the recommendations of the Secretary of the Interior.”. President Grant's endorsement approving the recommendation printed at 1 Kappler 811 (same instrument as the preceding entry).

fact.land_area: White Mountain Indian Reservation (enlarged by San Carlos division), Arizona
fact.note: The instrument reads: “withheld from sale and added to the White Mountain Indian Reservation in said Territory, which addition shall hereafter be known as the “San Carlos division of the”. Enlargement; the order recites the "White Mountain Indian Reservation as now established" and sets out its whole boundary.

fact.land_area: Winnebago Reservation, Nebraska (land ceded by the Omaha, Mar. 6, 1865)
fact.instrument: Treaty with the Winnebago, Mar. 8, 1865, art. II, 14 Stat. 671, 672
fact.note: The instrument reads: “the United States agree to set apart for the ... occupation and future home of the Winnebago Indians, forever”. Land taken from the Omaha cession of Mar. 6, 1865.

fact.land_area: Winnemucca Colony, Nevada (NE 1/4 sec. 32, T. 36 N., R. 38 E.)
fact.note: The instrument reads: “set aside for the use of two certain bands of homeless Shoshone Indians now residing near the towns of Winnemucca and Battle Mountain”. Order names the Winnemucca Band and Battle Mountain Band; the same order created the Battle Mountain tract (Te-Moak Tribe). Later enlarged (Exec. Order No. 2803 of 1918).

fact.instrument: Treaty with the Yankton Sioux, Apr. 19, 1858, art. I, 11 Stat. 743, 744
fact.note: The instrument reads: “except four hundred ... thousand acres thereof, situated and described as follows”. Reserved tract on the Missouri River, mouth of the Choteau (Chouteau) Creek north.

The instrument reads: “withdrawn from sale and set apart as a reservation for the use and occupancy of the Zuni Pueblo Indians”. Enlarged and defined by Exec. Orders of May 1, 1883 and Mar. 3, 1885 (1 Kappler 880); the Zuni Pueblo grant itself was confirmed under the Act of Dec. 22, 1858 (11 Stat. 374, not read).
